questions.stem: A 42-year-old man presented with a perianal lesion. He was known to have HIV infection (last CD4 count of 20 cells/μL, HIV-RNA viral load of 1.2 million). The lesion had been present for over 2.5 years and had previously responded to aciclovir or valaciclovir but had never completely healed. On this occasion, the painful ulcer had not responded to a 10-day course of oral valaciclovir 1 gram twice daily followed by a 14-day course of oral aciclovir 400 mg three times a day that was prescribed at the local STD clinic. The patient reported adherence to both regimens. DNA sequencing for resistance mutations cannot be obtained.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation: IV foscarnet The patient is likely infected with a thymidine kinase (TK)deficient virus, and the virus is resistant to high-dose aciclovir, valaciclovir, famciclovir, ganciclovir, or valganciclovir. Foscarnet is the drug of choice in thymidine kinase-deficient HSV . Alternatively, cidofovir can also be used, but it is much more nephrotoxic than foscarnet. Topical compound cidofovir creams can also be used, but this is not commercially available. Ribavirin has no activity against the herpes viruses.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 2 Q7

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman presented with a 3-day history of worsening headache. She had no past medical history of note but worked as an air hostess. Recent flights had been to New York, Los Angeles, and Paris. She was married with one teenage son and had not had any new sexual partners. She did not have any oral or genital ulceration on specific questioning. She had had similar illnesses on at least two other occasions. On examination she was photophobic with mild neck stiffness. She was alert and cognitively intact. Investigations: Peripheral white cell count 7.1 ×109/L CSF white cell count 342 ×106/L; 99% lymphocytes CSF protein 1012 mg/L CSF/plasma glucose 2.6/5.2 mmol/L CSF microscopy: no organisms seen
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely causative organism?
questions.explanation: HSV-2 Aseptic meningitis may be caused by HSV , enterovirus, CMV , and B. burgdorferi; however, the recurrent nature of the episodes of meningitis make this much more likely to be HSV-2. Recurrent meningococcal infections are recognized and occur due to a terminal complement deficiency; however, the CSF profile does not fit, she is older than would be expected for an inherited complement deficiency, and she has no risk factors for an acquired deficiency. Neuroborreliosis may present with an acute or chronic meningitis, but recurrent episodes would be unusual. HSV-2 meningitis may present in the absence of genital lesions; humans are the only known reservoir, but the vast majority of genital HSV infections are unrecognized (approx. 85%–90%). The first episode of HSV-2 meningitis usually occurs within 2 weeks of primary genital HSV infection. It is more common in women than men. The incidence of recurrent meningitis is reported to be around 30%. Lack of prior HSV-1 infection may predispose to more symptomatic HSV-2 infection, both genital and meningeal.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 2 Q11

questions.stem: A 21-year-old man presented with new penile lesions. He had insertive vaginal and oral intercourse using a latex condom with a casual female partner 72 hours earlier. He denied any current medications, known past medical history, or allergies. He was a college student and worked parttime in a chemistry laboratory. On examination, there were erythematous plaques over the shaft and glans penis.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Psoriasis Genital psoriasis can cause significant distress and is often confused with sexually transmitted infections. It has been estimated that the first presentation of psoriasis is genital in as many as 2%–5% of cases, making it a diagnosis that Infectious Disease clinicians may encounter. The lesions develop due to the Koebner phenomenon or “isomorphic response,” which describes the development of skin lesions in sites of skin trauma (in this case friction associated with coitus) that may be seen in psoriasis. There is no history of latex allergy in the setting of likely prior contact (“works in a laboratory,” no history of food allergies), nor are the lesions or time course a good fit for primary syphilis, HIV , or HSV .
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 2 Q48

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman presented with a new genital rash. The lesions were associated with mild burning. She had a history of orolabial cold sores. She and her male sex partner of 2 years reported no other concurrent sex partners. They used barrier contraception with condoms, and she was taking the combined oral contraceptive pill. On examination, a vulvar rash was observed
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: New acquisition of HSV-2 Symptoms associated with HSV-2 infection vary wildly. Primary episode outbreaks are associated with initial infection and are typically more severe than recurrences. Nonprimary first episode of genital herpes (i.e., in a patient who already has oral herpes as this patient does) may be less severe or asymptomatic. Typically there are fewer lesions and fewer systemic symptoms. In patients presenting with lesions concerning for genital herpes, HSV-2 and HSV-1 NAAT or culture should be performed on specimens obtained from the lesion(s). Concurrently serologic testing should be performed. Positive culture or NAAT without antibody is consistent with recent infection. Positive culture with antibody is consistent with longer infection. Testing her current partner might be helpful but if he were positive, it would not delineate whether she acquired HSV from him. The rash will spontaneously resolve. However, it may recur. Latex allergies are less likely to present with localized findings like this. T. pallidum is possible but typically presents with one ulcer and most often without itching or pain. (Image from Patel R. Genital herpes. Medicine, 2014;42(7),354–358.)
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 6 Q10

questions.stem: A 65-year-old woman presented with headache, agitation, and delirium. She had a witnessed generalized seizure in the emergency department. She was started on antiepileptic medication, and head CT was performed to evaluate for stroke. The head CT was within normal limits. Brain MRI was later performed, and it demonstrated bilateral temporal lobe enhancement.
questions.lead_in: What test would be most likely to prove the correct diagnosis?
questions.explanation: CSF HSV PCR This patient likely has HSV-1 encephalitis. Disproportionate enhancement of the temporal lobes, as demonstrated on her MRI, is characteristic. Behavioral abnormalities and new-onset seizures are also common.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 8 Q31

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man presents with acute unilateral vision loss. On funduscopic examination, he has significant vitreitis and retinal findings concerning for acute retinal necrosis.
questions.explanation: Aciclovir Acute retinal necrosis is most often caused by varicella zoster virus, and therapy with aciclovir should be administered. Corticosteroids may be used to decrease ocular inflammation but should not be given until after antiviral therapy is initiated.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 7 Q30

questions.model_answer: (1) Herpes simplex virus (HSV-1 or HSV-2); (2) Varicella-zoster virus. Both are alphaherpesviruses and are morphologically identical on electron microscopy — all herpesviruses share a double-stranded DNA core, an icosahedral capsid of 162 capsomers, tegument, lipid envelope with surface glycoproteins, and a diameter of about 160 nm — so EM cannot distinguish them; typing requires PCR/culture.

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Skin, eye and mouth (localized cutaneous/mucocutaneous) disease — cutaneous involvement alone carries no mortality but subclinical CNS infection may coexist; (2) CNS disease (encephalitis); (3) Disseminated/visceral disease. Untreated, more than 70% disseminate or develop CNS infection, with 65% overall mortality and fewer than 20% of CNS cases developing normally.
b) Primary/newly acquired maternal HSV near term: 30%–50%. Reactivation (recurrent) HSV at delivery: <1% (only ~2% of HSV-2 seropositive women shed at delivery, and only ~1% of exposed infants become infected).
c) Active lesions on the cervix or external genitalia at delivery are an indication for abdominal (cesarean) delivery; treat the lesions, avoid fetal scalp electrodes (OR 3.5 for transmission), and observe/evaluate the infant.
d) Treat the acquisition with acyclovir 400 mg PO three times daily or valacyclovir 500–1000 mg PO twice daily for 7–10 days. At delivery, examine the external genitalia and cervix early in labour with a swab for HSV; if no lesions are present a vaginal delivery is appropriate by Mandell, but because first-episode exposure occurred, the infant should have PCR/cultures of throat, nasopharynx, eyes and rectum and many authorities would start IV acyclovir empirically.
e) Cesarean section is not warranted for all women with recurrent genital herpes. Advise early presentation in labour for careful examination of the external genitalia and cervix plus a swab; vaginal delivery if no lesions, abdominal delivery if active lesions; avoid scalp electrodes; treat symptomatic recurrences.
questions.beyond_mandell: SOGC/ACOG: offer cesarean for primary genital HSV acquired in the third trimester even without lesions at delivery, and suppressive acyclovir/valacyclovir from 36 weeks for recurrent genital herpes — neither is stated in this Mandell chapter.
questions.cohort_conflict: Cohort quotes up to 60% transmission with primary infection; Mandell states 30%–50% for acquisition near term and <1% (not <2%) for reactivation.

cohort_answer.text:
Three clinical syndromes: Skin, eye and mucuous membrane infection; Localized central nervous system; Disseminated
% vertical transmission: Primary: up to 60% (as per CPS statement); First episode non-primary: ≤30%; Recurrent: <2%
Term with active recurrence lesions: C-section
Women with primary genital herpes in the third trimester of pregnancy have a high risk of transmitting HSV to their neonates and should be counselled accordingly and should be offered a Caesarean section to decrease this risk. Can be placed on ppx 36 weeks onwards.
Woman with recurrent lesions: Treatment for active episode, then offered acyclovir or valacyclovir suppression at 36 weeks' gestation to decrease the risk of clinical lesions and viral shedding at the time of delivery and therefore decrease the need for Caesarean section.

questions.model_answer:
a) First-episode genital herpes with HSV aseptic meningitis; pathogen HSV-2 (overt viral meningitis is much more commonly HSV-2 than HSV-1). Meningeal symptoms begin 3–12 days after genital lesions; 36% of women with primary genital HSV-2 have headache, stiff neck and photophobia, and 6.4% require admission.
b) (1) Inoculation of virus onto susceptible mucosa or abraded skin of the genital tract with replication in epidermal and dermal cells; (2) infection of sensory (and autonomic) nerve endings and intraaxonal retrograde transport of the nucleocapsid to the sacral (S2–S5) dorsal root ganglia, where high-level replication occurs and latency is established; (3) centrifugal spread back along peripheral sensory nerves to mucocutaneous surfaces, producing new lesion crops distant from the initial vesicles; (4) extension into the CNS/meninges by neural spread, aided by the viremia present in about 25% of primary HSV-2 infections, giving lymphocytic meningitis.
c) (1) Aseptic (lymphocytic) meningitis; (2) Mollaret benign recurrent lymphocytic meningitis; (3) transverse myelitis; (4) sacral radiculopathy/autonomic dysfunction (urinary retention, constipation, perineal hyperesthesia or anesthesia, impotence). Also HSV encephalitis and Bell palsy.
d) Yes. She has genital, not hand or orolabial, lesions; transmission requires contact with infected secretions, and HSV is readily inactivated at room temperature so aerosol and fomite spread are unusual. She may return once clinically well, with lesions covered and strict hand hygiene; treat with IV acyclovir 10 mg/kg every 8 hours if hospitalized for meningitis. Staff with uncovered external HSV lesions (especially orolabial) or herpetic whitlow must not have intimate contact with neonates.
questions.beyond_mandell: Return-to-work timing is a CDC/SHEA healthcare-personnel recommendation; Mandell only addresses restricting staff with external lesions from contact with neonates.

cohort_answer.text: Diagnosis: Genital HSV (Redbook: HSV infection also can manifest as mild, self-limited aseptic meningitis, usually associated with genital HSV-2 infection; ~25% of primary HSV2 can have aseptic meningitis). Pathogenesis: Most viral pathogens affecting the CNS initially infect mucosal surfaces followed by viral replication in regional lymph nodes; subsequently, primary viremia that signals the onset of illness and subsequent seeding of other organs; except for neonatal HSV infection, most viruses reach the CNS during a second viremia that follows viral replication in other organs, particularly the liver and spleen. Neurological complications: Transverse myelitis; Encephalitis; Bell's palsy; Ascending myelitis; Mollaret meningitis (recurrent aseptic meningitis); Acute retinal necrosis. Return to work: Transmission of HSV infection from health care professionals with genital lesions is not likely as long as they comply with hand hygiene policies; can return to work once well

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Localized skin, eye and mouth disease (vesicular skin lesions, keratoconjunctivitis/chorioretinitis, oral ulcers); (2) CNS disease/encephalitis; (3) Disseminated visceral disease presenting as neonatal sepsis with hepatitis, pneumonitis and adrenal involvement. Note many infants have no visible skin lesions until late in the course.
b) High — 30% to 50% when the mother acquires HSV near term; risk is further increased by HSV-1 rather than HSV-2 (OR 35), cervical rather than vulvar shedding (OR 15) and fetal scalp electrodes (OR 3.5).
c) Very low. Reactivation at delivery carries <1% transmission, and abdominal delivery is protective (OR 0.14); an infant delivered by cesarean before rupture of membranes is at minimal risk.
d) A septic-appearing neonate has disseminated HSV disease; regardless of maternal stage, evaluate immediately (surface PCR/cultures, blood and CSF HSV PCR, liver enzymes) and start empirical high-dose IV acyclovir before results return, since untreated neonatal herpes carries 65% mortality.

questions.model_answer:
a) 30% to 50% when HSV is acquired near term.
b) <1% with reactivation at delivery (only ~2% of HSV-2 seropositive women shed at delivery and ~1% of exposed infants are infected).
c) Acyclovir, 60 mg/kg/day intravenously divided into three daily doses (20 mg/kg IV q8h), for 21 days — 14 days if disease is limited to skin/cutaneous involvement — followed by oral acyclovir suppression for 6 months, which improves neurodevelopmental outcome.
d) (1) Throat/mouth; (2) nasopharynx; (3) eyes (conjunctivae); (4) rectum. Obtain immediately and repeat at 5- to 10-day intervals; any infant from whom HSV is isolated more than 24 hours after delivery is treated with IV acyclovir.
e) (1) Skin/eye/mouth (cutaneous) disease — 14 days IV acyclovir; (2) CNS disease — 21 days; (3) Disseminated visceral disease — 21 days. All followed by 6 months of oral acyclovir suppression. (True congenital, in utero infection accounts for only 5%–8% of neonatal herpes and presents with microcephaly, hydrocephalus and chorioretinitis.)

questions.model_answer:
a) Disseminated herpes simplex virus infection with HSV hepatitis. HSV hepatitis is characterized by fever, abrupt marked elevation of aminotransferases and bilirubin, and leukopenia (<4000 white blood cells/µL), often with disseminated intravascular coagulation; pregnancy predisposes to severe visceral dissemination of primary genital HSV, and mucocutaneous lesions may be absent. Diagnose with blood HSV PCR.
b) Intravenous acyclovir immediately — 10 mg/kg IV every 8 hours (renally adjusted); disseminated visceral infection in pregnant and immunosuppressed patients carries high mortality and should be treated without waiting for confirmation.
questions.cohort_conflict: The cohort answered hepatitis A/E (ribavirin, which is contraindicated in pregnancy) or hepatitis B; Mandell's picture of fever, transaminases in the thousands and leukopenia in a pregnant woman is classic disseminated HSV hepatitis treated with IV acyclovir.

cohort_answer.text: Infection: ?Hepatitis A or Hepatitis E - ribavirin (note: ribavirin is Pregnancy Category X, contraindicated in pregnancy); alternative teaching point suggests this may be Hepatitis B. Treatment: Supportive; immunization of contacts; ?PEG IFN for chronic Hep D; Ribavirin for severe acute and chronic Hep E in SOT; Hep E vaccine licensed in China. For Hep B in pregnancy: Tenofovir (TDF) 300mg po daily.

questions.model_answer:
a) Examine the external genitalia and cervix carefully in early labour and swab for HSV PCR. With no lesions, Mandell supports vaginal delivery, avoiding fetal scalp electrodes; because this is first-episode exposure, the infant needs throat, nasopharynx, eye and rectal PCR/culture immediately and at 5- to 10-day intervals, close observation for the first month, and many authorities would start empirical IV acyclovir.
b) Mother: active lesions on the cervix or external genitalia are an indication for abdominal (cesarean) delivery; treat with acyclovir 400 mg PO three times daily or valacyclovir 500–1000 mg PO twice daily for 7–10 days to reduce maternal dissemination; avoid scalp electrodes; because extragenital lesions are frequent with late-pregnancy primary infection, separate mother and infant until she has a clinical and virologic response. Baby: isolate, obtain surface PCR/cultures, liver function tests and CSF examination, and start IV acyclovir empirically — do not wait for results.
c) <1% with reactivation at delivery; only ~2% of HSV-2 seropositive women shed at delivery and only ~1% of exposed infants become infected. Cesarean section is therefore not warranted for all women with recurrent disease. Nonetheless 30%–50% of all neonatal HSV cases are born to mothers with established genital herpes.
d) Acyclovir 60 mg/kg/day IV divided q8h: 14 days for disease limited to skin/cutaneous involvement, 21 days for CNS or disseminated disease, followed by 6 months of oral acyclovir suppression to improve neurodevelopmental outcome.
questions.beyond_mandell: SOGC/ACOG advise offering cesarean delivery for primary genital HSV acquired in the third trimester even without lesions in labour, and suppressive antivirals from 36 weeks; this chapter does not state either.
questions.cohort_conflict: The cohort advises cesarean for the 32-week primary infection with no lesions at delivery; Mandell states women with no evidence of lesions should have a vaginal delivery (the cesarean recommendation is a guideline position, not a Mandell one).

cohort_answer.text:
If no current active lesions: advise/discuss C-section; swab baby mucous membranes within 24hrs of delivery for HSV PCR; send baby home if doing well while awaiting PCR; if symptoms or PCR+ then re-admit and start Acyclovir, get blood/CSF PCR; if blood/CSF positive Acyclovir x21 days, if negative x14d
For mother: assess for active lesions/prodromal symptoms; if present offer C-section ASAP; if absent discuss risk/benefit of C-section; avoid/limit scalp electrodes. For baby: vaginal delivery, swab and NAT blood/CSF at delivery; treat with Acyclovir while awaiting testing if mom has lesions; if asymptomatic no treatment/no routine swabs, educate parents
Recurrent HSV: if lesions present 2-5%, if no lesions 0.02-0.05%. Non-primary first genital episode: <30%. Primary infection, particularly late in pregnancy: 30-60%. Risk factors: nature of infection (primary ~60%, recurrent <2%), mode of delivery, duration of ROM, intrapartum instrumentation, neonatal factors. Maternal prophylaxis with valacyclovir/acyclovir from 36 weeks until delivery for recurrent infection
If LP+ or blood+: treat 21 days minimum IV acyclovir. If blood/CSF negative but swabs positive: 14 days. If all negative: 10 days if high risk. Repeat LP near end of 21 days for CNS disease. Ophthalmology check, trifluridine if ocular infection. CNS/disseminated HSV after negative LP - switch to oral suppressive acyclovir for 6 months

questions.model_answer:
a) Genital herpes with HSV aseptic (lymphocytic) meningitis; pathogen HSV-2 — both types have been isolated from CSF but overt viral meningitis is much more common with HSV-2. Confirm with CSF HSV PCR; CSF shows 10–1000 cells/mm3, lymphocyte predominant, glucose >50% of serum, mildly raised protein.
b) (1) Inoculation and replication in genital epidermal/dermal cells; (2) infection of sensory nerve endings with intraaxonal retrograde transport of nucleocapsid to the sacral S2–S5 dorsal root ganglia, high-level ganglionic replication and establishment of latency; (3) centrifugal spread through peripheral sensory nerves back to mucocutaneous surfaces, producing new distant lesion crops; (4) neural extension to the meninges/CNS, facilitated by the viremia present in about 25% of primary HSV-2 infections, causing lymphocytic meningitis.
c) (1) Mollaret benign recurrent lymphocytic meningitis (HSV-2 causes most recurrent cases); (2) transverse myelitis; (3) sacral radiculopathy with autonomic dysfunction (urinary retention, constipation, perineal anesthesia, impotence, atonic bladder); (4) HSV encephalitis (HSV-1 causes >95%, 10%–20% of sporadic encephalitis). Also Bell palsy.
d) Yes. Her lesions are genital and covered; HSV spreads by direct contact with infected secretions and is readily inactivated by drying and room temperature, so aerosol/fomite spread is unusual. She may resume work once clinically recovered, with lesions covered and meticulous hand hygiene; the occupational hazards are orolabial lesions and herpetic whitlow, and staff with external HSV lesions must avoid intimate contact with neonates. Treat symptomatic hospitalized meningitis with IV acyclovir 10 mg/kg q8h for 7–10 days; offer suppression if meningitis recurs.
questions.beyond_mandell: Precise return-to-work and precaution requirements come from CDC/SHEA healthcare-personnel guidance, not this chapter.

cohort_answer.text: Diagnosis: HSV-2 meningitis (recurrence = Mollaret's); treat only if immunosuppressed (acyclovir 10mg/kg IV q8h or valacyclovir 500mg PO BID x7 days); can offer suppressive therapy. Pathogenesis: viral contact with mucosa/broken skin and replication at site; retrograde ascension up sensory neuron to dorsal root ganglion establishing latency; reactivation causes anterograde travel to site near primary infection; virus can travel across synapses into CNS causing meningitis/encephalitis. Other complications: Encephalitis, Transverse myelitis, Trigeminal neuralgia (HSV-1), Post-infectious encephalomyelitis, Peripheral neuritis, Temporal lobe epilepsy. Return to work: Yes - initially needs contact/droplet until etiology confirmed by PCR, then can resume work with lesions covered; viral meningitis (adult) routine precautions, (peds) contact until enterovirus ruled out

questions.model_answer:
Syndromes: (1) skin/eye/mouth disease (14 days IV acyclovir); (2) CNS disease/encephalitis (21 days); (3) disseminated visceral disease (21 days); all followed by 6 months of oral acyclovir suppression. Untreated, >70% disseminate or involve the CNS, with 65% mortality; 90% of neonatal herpes is perinatally acquired, 5%–8% congenital (microcephaly, hydrocephalus, chorioretinitis).
Transmission risk: maternal acquisition near term 30%–50%; reactivation/recurrent HSV at delivery <1% (2% of HSV-2 seropositive women shed at delivery, 1% of exposed infants infected).
Active lesions in labour, membranes intact: active lesions on the cervix or external genitalia are an indication for cesarean delivery; swab for HSV, avoid fetal scalp electrodes, treat the mother, isolate the infant with surface cultures/PCR, liver function tests and CSF examination, and observe closely for the first month.
Primary HSV in the third trimester, no lesions in labour: treat the acquisition with acyclovir 400 mg PO tid or valacyclovir 500–1000 mg PO bid for 7–10 days; examine and swab in early labour; Mandell supports vaginal delivery if no lesions are present. Because this is first-episode exposure, the infant should have throat, nasopharynx, eye and rectal PCR at delivery and at 5- to 10-day intervals, and many authorities start empirical IV acyclovir.
Recurrent HSV, no current lesions: no cesarean section — it is not warranted for all women with recurrent genital disease; weekly virologic monitoring and amniocentesis are not recommended as antepartum shedding does not predict shedding at term. Advise early presentation in labour for examination of the external genitalia and cervix plus swab, vaginal delivery if no lesions, and avoid fetal scalp electrodes.
questions.beyond_mandell: SOGC/ACOG advise cesarean for third-trimester primary genital HSV and suppressive acyclovir/valacyclovir from 36 weeks for recurrent disease; neither appears in this chapter.
questions.cohort_conflict: The cohort recommends cesarean for third-trimester primary infection with no lesions at delivery and suppressive therapy from 36 weeks; Mandell states that women with no lesions should deliver vaginally and does not endorse routine cesarean or 36-week suppression.

cohort_answer.text:
SEM - skin, eyes, mucous membranes (tx 14 days), 45%, high risk progression if untreated, anytime before 6 weeks. Localized CNS HSV (tx 21 days), 30%, usually 2nd-3rd week of life (up to 6 weeks). Disseminated HSV (tx 21 days), sepsis-like with end organ involvement (liver, lungs, CNS, heart, adrenals, bone marrow, renal, GI, skin). Intra-uterine HSV (<5%, very rare)
Primary HSV 25-60% (60% if primary infection at time of birth). First episode non-primary <30%. Recurrent infection <2%. Presents within 6 weeks of life
Women with active lesions or prodrome at delivery should be offered elective C/S. If ROM occurs, C/S ideally within 4 hours. If delivery imminent, no benefit to C/S. Contact precautions for mom during labor, delivery, postpartum
Woman with primary HSV any time during 3rd trimester -> C/S recommended (ACOG and RCOG UK)
Offer suppressive antiviral at or beyond 36 weeks gestation (acyclovir or valacyclovir); C/S not required; avoid scalp electrodes/fetal scalp monitoring/vacuum/forceps if possible. Infant: observe for signs of NHSV, does not require ACV therapy, mucous membrane swabs not routinely recommended

B) Explain the pathogenesis of CNS infection

questions.model_answer:
a) HSV-2 aseptic (lymphocytic) meningitis complicating primary genital herpes. Overt viral meningitis is far more common with HSV-2 than HSV-1; meningeal symptoms typically begin 3-12 days after genital lesions, with clear CSF, 10-1000 WBC/mm3 lymphocyte-predominant pleocytosis, normal/near-normal glucose and mildly elevated protein.
b) After mucocutaneous replication at the genital site, virus enters sacral sensory nerve endings and travels by axonal transport to the sacral dorsal root ganglia, where latency is established; virus reaching the neuraxis/subarachnoid space produces meningeal inflammation. Plasma viremia is commonly demonstrated during primary infection, so hematogenous seeding also contributes. Diagnosis is by CSF HSV PCR, which is considerably more sensitive than CSF culture.
c) Yes. Genital HSV is not a bar to patient care: the lesions must be covered and meticulous hand hygiene and gloves observed (gloving is why occupational herpetic whitlow has become uncommon). The relevant restriction is that personnel with uncovered/external HSV lesions should not have intimate contact with neonates, so she should avoid direct contact with newborns until lesions are crusted.
d) (1) Benign recurrent lymphocytic (Mollaret) meningitis - recurrent 3-7 day episodes, HSV-2 responsible for most cases. (2) Sacral autonomic radiculopathy - perineal hyperesthesia/anesthesia, urinary retention, constipation, atonic bladder, usually resolving in 4-8 weeks. (3) Transverse myelitis with lower-limb weakness and depressed reflexes. (4) HSV encephalitis (predominantly HSV-1), the commonest cause of sporadic focal encephalitis; Bell palsy is a further recognized complication.

cohort_answer.text:
A) HSV-2 meningitis. Viral meningitis in immunocompetent adults is generally caused by HSV-2. Genital lesions present in 85% of patients with primary HSV-2 meningitis and precede onset of CNS sx by 7 days. CSF profile: pleocytosis with predominance of lymphocytes, normal glucose.

B) HSV invades through peripheral nerves (sacral nerves in this case). Once within the CNS, viruses spread through the subarachnoid space in CSF, causing an inflammatory response leading to meningitis; may also spread directly or via inflammatory leukocytes through neural tissue to neurons and glial cells. Viruses enter the CNS via: (1) haematogenous spread after replicating outside the CNS (e.g. enteroviruses), crossing the blood-brain barrier directly or carried in infected leukocytes (mumps, measles, herpesviruses), infecting vascular endothelial cells - note HSV-2 viraemia is common in primary infection; (2) invasion through peripheral and cranial nerves (as for polio and HSV respectively).

C) Yes - HCWs with genital HSV infection do not have to inform OHS of these conditions. There should be no risk to patients as long as good hygiene is maintained, including meticulous hand hygiene, and lesions are covered.

D) Recurrent benign lymphocytic meningitis (Mollaret's meningitis) - transient neurological manifestations including seizures, hallucinations, diplopia, cranial nerve palsies, or altered consciousness in half of patients. Sacral Radiculopathy (Elsberg syndrome) - affects lumbar/sacral nerve roots, often recurrent, with radicular pain, paresthesias, urinary retention, constipation, anogenital discomfort, leg weakness. Bell's Palsy. Transverse myelitis (not encephalitis - that is mostly caused by HSV-1).

questions.model_answer:
a) Disseminated HSV infection with HSV hepatitis. HSV hepatitis presents with fever, abrupt elevation of aminotransferases and bilirubin, and leukopenia (<4000/uL), may be complicated by DIC, and pregnancy predisposes to severe visceral dissemination of primary genital HSV (third-trimester dissemination is described); anicteric hepatitis with very high transaminases is characteristic. questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Cesarean delivery when active lesions are present on the cervix or external genitalia (or prodromal symptoms) at the onset of labour - she should come to hospital early in labour for careful genital/cervical examination plus swab for HSV; abdominal delivery is protective (OR 0.14) and women with no lesions deliver vaginally. (2) Suppressive antiviral therapy in late pregnancy (from 36 weeks) with acyclovir or valacyclovir to reduce recurrences and shedding at delivery; also avoid fetal scalp electrodes (OR 3.5) and prolonged rupture of membranes. Weekly antenatal viral cultures and amniocentesis are not recommended.
b) With recurrent/reactivated HSV-2 at delivery the risk is low, <1%-2%; in a woman who acquires HSV near term the risk is 30%-50%, highest with primary HSV-1 genital infection.
questions.beyond_mandell: Suppressive therapy starting at 36 weeks is an ACOG/Red Book recommendation; the slice supports antiviral treatment in pregnancy but not the 36-week start.

cohort_answer.text: A) C/S at delivery if prodromal sx or presence of active lesions; if recurrent genital HSV, offer suppressive acyclovir/valacyclovir at 36 weeks gestation (Red book, ACOG). B) 25-60% in mother who develops primary HSV infection near time of delivery (60% for primary, <30% if first episode non-primary); if mom has reactivation earlier than first half of pregnancy, risk is <2%.

parts.text: Give four neurologic complications.
What is the most common mechanism of resistance to acyclovir?

parts_raw.text: A. 4 neurologic complications:
B. most common mechanism of resistance to acyclovir:

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Aseptic (lymphocytic) meningitis, mainly HSV-2 - hospitalization in 6.4% of women and 1.6% of men with primary genital HSV-2. (2) Benign recurrent lymphocytic (Mollaret) meningitis, HSV-2. (3) HSV encephalitis, predominantly HSV-1, the most commonly identified cause of acute sporadic viral encephalitis. (4) Sacral autonomic radiculopathy/transverse myelitis - urinary retention, constipation, perineal hyperesthesia, lower-limb weakness (Bell palsy and acute retinal necrosis are further recognized complications).
b) Mutation of the viral thymidine kinase gene, giving absent, reduced or altered-specificity TK so acyclovir cannot undergo its initial phosphorylation. Resistance emerges sequentially in immunocompromised hosts who do not control mucosal infection and presents as chronic progressive ulcerative mucocutaneous disease with prolonged shedding.

cohort_answer.text:
A: Aseptic meningitis (HSV1 and HSV2). Mollaret's meningitis (HSV-2). Encephalitis (HSV-1). Transverse myelitis (HSV-2 and 1). Sacral radiculitis (HSV-2, with acute urinary retention called Elsberg syndrome, extremely rare). Acute retinal necrosis (HSV-1?). Cranial neuropathy (HSV-1 - Bell's palsy)

B: Thymidine kinase mutations (90-95% of Acyclovir resistance). Acyclovir must be phosphorylated first by the viral thymidine kinase (TK) and then by cellular kinases before inhibiting the virus-encoded DNA polymerase (DNA pol). Resistant HSV infection usually characterized by a chronic, progressive ulcerative mucocutaneous disease with prolonged shedding of virus in immunocompromised hosts

parts.text: Give three syndromes of HSV in the first 30 days of life.

questions.model_answer: (1) Skin, eye and mouth (SEM) disease - cutaneous involvement only, not associated with mortality, though subclinical CNS infection may coexist. (2) Localized CNS disease (encephalitis), with or without skin/eye/mouth involvement - fewer than 20% of neonates with CNS infection develop normally. (3) Disseminated visceral disease, most prominently liver and lungs, frequently with CNS involvement; neonates have the highest frequency of visceral/CNS infection of any HSV-infected group and untreated mortality is 65%.

cohort_answer.text: In newborn infants, herpes simplex virus (HSV) infection can manifest as: (1) Disseminated disease involving multiple organs, most prominently liver and lungs, and in 60% to 75% of cases also involving the central nervous system (CNS) - 25% of cases (2) CNS disease localized CNS disease, with or without skin, eye, or mouth involvement - 30% of cases (3) SEM disease (skin, eyes, and/or mouth) - 45% of cases (Red book)
